item.title: Victor Glover, Artemis II astronaut, joins Cal Poly in leadership role - USA Today
item.description:
Victor Glover, Artemis II astronaut, joins Cal Poly in leadership role

From piloting NASA’s Artemis II mission around the Moon to retelling his tales to the world, California native and astronaut Victor Glover announced that he will be hanging up his boots after accepting a full-time administrative leadership position at his alma mater, California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo.

In this new role, Glover will focus on building the university's partnerships, philanthropy, and long-term strategies, hoping to elevate the Cal Poly and Cal Poly Maritime Academy campuses into global leaders "in polytechnic education, research innovation and workforce production."

"There are a lot of neat opportunities as we work to, you know, grow our science and industrial base, our partnerships with other universities, and our partnerships with corporate America," Glover said in an interview with USA TODAY.

"What's really cool is I get to do that for Cal Poly, and I'm also in this emeritus program, which allows people with unique experiences to continue to serve NASA in a different capacity."

Specifically, NASA allows individuals like Glover and Reid Wiseman, commander of the 2026 Artemis II lunar flyby mission, to step down from their roles with the agency while continuing to support the country's space program by training and mentoring the next generation of scientists.

“As I grow into this new role, NASA and spaceflight remain a meaningful part of my journey of service,” Glover told NASA in an interview about his new position. “I’m excited to keep uplifting my friends and cheering them on as they reach for the Moon. Together, we’ll keep pushing boundaries and inspiring the next giant leap.”

In this new role, Glover will be spending much of his time guiding the university's president, provost, college deans, and other university leaders to develop and expand the university’s leadership in engineering, applied computing, aerospace, aviation, maritime, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and national defense.

However, between these meetings, Glover shared his desire to stand in front of an auditorium and teach the next generation by recounting his nearly 14 years as an active astronaut and 28-year career in the United States Navy.

Many may assume that Glover would want to focus his lessons on space and putting a person on the Moon; but he told USA TODAY that, "at the end of the day, I probably would love to teach a course on communication."

"That's something that I think young technical professionals need to really get as good at as the technical skills to be a tech leader, to be a science leader. And to be a public servant, I think communication is one of the most important roles that we get to serve in," Glover said.

He highlighted how his ability to communicate efficiently was a pivotal skill throughout his career, from his time in the military to NASA.

"In the early 2000s, when I was a test pilot, I was a project officer as well. So it wasn't just about flying test missions. I was part of a team with some really challenging goals that, you know, ended with making sure our service members stayed safe in combat and during training. And so we had to come together and tackle these really big problems," Glover said.

"I wasn't the most technical person on the team, but I really brought the teamwork and the leadership and the communication to the front and made sure that that was something that we were constantly thinking about."

Why did Glover choose to return to Cal Poly?

Although one might assume it would be a no-brainer to accept an administrative role at a top university, Glover shared how important his time at Cal Poly was to his life trajectory.

Not only did Glover receive the foundational education that would one day lead him to becoming a historic figure, but it's also where he met his wife, Dionna Odom Glover, of 30 years at Cal Poly.

"We spent a lot of time driving up and down the coast, tutoring for a program called MESA, Mathematics, Engineering, and Science Achievement. And so we spent so much time together doing that job and also sitting in the university union there, right outside the Chumash Auditorium on campus. And we would just talk," Glover said.

At Cal Poly, Glover's career goal also changed drastically. Initially, he planned to pursue a career in "conceptual automotive design," but one of his college mentors, a Navy reservist, convinced Glover to enlist in the military.

With his father's support, Glover changed his military aspiration of becoming a Navy SEAL and traded it for a lifetime in the skies and in space.

"My dad said to me in 1997, with an engineering degree from Cal Poly and wings of gold, you never know, you might mess around and become an astronaut," Glover said.

"So the lesson is, listen to your parents, kids."

"But it was really my dad's suggestion. And I took a huge leap of faith there. And I took a leap of faith to apply to be an astronaut," he added.

Years later, on June 15, 2025, Glover returned to Cal Poly to accept an honorary Doctor of Science degree from the College of Engineering.

Through his life experience, Glover learned the value of one phrase, "we are a team," and hopes to teach students and leaders at Cal Poly the importance of that idea, and hopefully teach people around the world the importance of working together for a better tomorrow.

"You know, when you get to see your home from far away, you know, that saying, absence makes the heart grow fonder. It's so true. And that distance also can make the heart grow fonder. And so seeing our planet from the space station helped me appreciate how connected this system was, how we, you know, Earth is one system that works together," Glover said.

"It's truly a system. But then seeing it from the moon hanging there in the blackness of space with the Milky Way as the background just really hit home that we are on a spaceship and that we are in this really beautiful oasis on this crude ship that we call Earth, and that we're a crew, like the country, the planet, humanity."

USA TODAY video producer Kat Filardi contributed to this article.

item.title: NASA reveals Artemis III astronaut crew - Axios
item.description:
NASA reveals Artemis III astronaut crew

The Artemis III crew. From left: Andre Douglas, Luca Parmitano, Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio. Photo: NASA/Bill Stafford

NASA on Tuesday revealed the four-person roster for Artemis III, the next mission in the space agency's quest to return humans to the Moon's surface.

Why it matters: Artemis III will involve key tests of one or both lunar landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin, in Earth orbit — similar to Apollo 9 before Apollo 11's historic Moon landing.

  • That's after NASA changed Artemis III to a test flight for the landers before a planned Moon landing with Artemis IV.

Driving the news: The Artemis III crew includes mission specialist and first-time astronaut Andre Douglas; mission specialist and record-setting astronaut U.S. Army Col. Frank Rubio, pilot Luca Parmitano (an Italian Air Force colonel and onetime International Space Station commander); and commander Randy Bresnik, a longtime NASA astronaut and former U.S. Marine Corps. colonel.

  • NASA astronaut Bob Hines is a backup crew member who will train alongside the main quartet in case he's needed.
  • All five astronauts involved are male — a departure from Artemis II, when Christina Koch became the first woman to travel beyond low Earth orbit.

The plan: Blue Origin's lander will be launched into Earth orbit first, followed by the four astronauts aboard an Orion spacecraft.

  • They'll rendezvous in space for docking and testing.

Orion will then detach and await SpaceX's Starship for similar docking and testing before the crew returns home to Earth.

  • The two-week mission is set for mid-2027.

What they're saying: "As the first crewed Artemis mission with commercial spacecraft, this test flight will enable us to prove we can carry out highly choreographed operations with our partners across hardware interfaces, software, propulsion systems, and life support elements with crew in the high-stakes space environment," NASA Moon-to-Mars Acting Assistant Deputy Associate Administrator Jeremy Parsons said during a press conference Tuesday.

Reality check: Neither SpaceX nor Blue Origin's landers are ready yet, and the Artemis III mission date could slip.

  • Last month's catastrophic explosion involving Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket also stands to complicate the timeline — though Blue Origin Senior Vice President John Couluris promised Tuesday that the company will be ready to launch in 2027.

NASA's Parsons echoed that sentiment, calling setbacks a "learning opportunity."

  • "We are confident that New Glenn will be ready for Artemis III," Parsons added.

What's next: TheArtemis IV lunar landing is still planned for early 2028 — but any delays for Artemis III could reverberate through the program.

Artemis III will launch four astronauts from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard the Orion spacecraft on the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. The mission will test critical rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems needed to deliver astronauts to the lunar surface. Building on the successful Artemis II crewed test flight in April, Artemis III will pave the way for future surface missions.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly complex missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.
